title: Rollout adds an HTTP readiness probe on a path that 404s

retrieved.title: CrashLoopBackOff
retrieved.text:
## Fixes

- If the command is wrong (for example a demo container that ends in `exit 1`), correct `command`/`args` or the image entrypoint so the main process stays in the foreground.
- If a config value is missing, add the env var or volume and roll the workload.
- If a dependency is down, fix that service or make startup retry instead of exiting.
- If a liveness probe is too aggressive, increase `initialDelaySeconds` / `failureThreshold` (see probe-failures).
- After a fix, roll the deployment and confirm the restart count stops climbing:

  ```bash
  kubectl rollout status deploy/<name> -n <ns>
  kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> --watch
  ```

retrieved.title: Liveness and readiness probe failures
retrieved.text:
## Fixes

- Increase `initialDelaySeconds`, `periodSeconds`, `timeoutSeconds`, or `failureThreshold` so slow starts can finish.
- Add or fix a `startupProbe` for apps that take a long time to boot, and keep liveness conservative.
- Point HTTP probes at a cheap, local endpoint that does not depend on downstream systems.
- Fix a wrong port or path rather than disabling the probe entirely.
- After changing probes, roll the deployment and confirm `READY` stays `1/1` and events stop showing `Unhealthy`.

retrieved.title: Liveness and readiness probe failures
retrieved.text:
## Diagnosis

1. Inspect the probe definitions and recent probe events:

   ```bash
   kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns>
   kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].livenessProbe}'
   kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].readinessProbe}'
   kubectl get endpoints <svc> -n <ns>
   ```

2. Exec into a running container (if it lives long enough) and call the same path or command the probe uses.
3. Read current and previous logs around the time of each restart. If the process is killed mid-startup, the liveness probe is a prime suspect.
4. Distinguish "app is crashing on its own" (see CrashLoopBackOff) from "kubelet is killing a healthy-but-slow process".

retrieved.title: DNS issues inside the cluster
retrieved.text:
## Symptoms

- Application logs show `unknown host`, `Name or service not known`, `no such host`, `i/o timeout` talking to a Service name, or repeated reconnects to a hostname that should exist.
- `nslookup` / `getent hosts` / `dig` from a debug container fail for `kubernetes.default` or for the target Service.
- CoreDNS pods in `kube-system` may be crash-looping, pending, or not ready. Nodes may show `NetworkUnavailable`.
- Traffic to raw ClusterIPs or pod IPs still works, which is a strong hint the problem is name resolution, not the network path itself.

retrieved.title: Pending and unschedulable pods
retrieved.text:
## Diagnosis

1. Read the `FailedScheduling` message first — it usually lists every reason a node was skipped:

   ```bash
   kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns>
   kubectl get events -n <ns> --field-selector reason=FailedScheduling
   ```

2. Compare requests to allocatable resources:

   ```bash
   kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].resources.requests}'
   kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,STATUS:.status.conditions[-1],CPU:.status.allocatable.cpu,MEM:.status.allocatable.memory
   kubectl describe node <node>
   ```

3. Check taints, affinity, and selectors on the pod against labels and taints on the nodes.
4. If the message mentions a PVC or volume, inspect the claim (see the PVC pending runbook).
